passage:
The worst moment wasn't the meeting. It was that evening, going through our old spreadsheets and realising Tejas had moved the customer list to a new company without telling me. I'm Vinita. Tejas was my closest friend before becoming my co-founder, so I doubted everything: the late nights, the first client, even the jokes.

I was so angry I nearly posted something online. Instead I let myself be sad first. Then I collected facts: dates, emails, the founders' agreement we'd signed. I wrote down what had actually been agreed. The work we built is real, whatever Tejas did. I'm not making any big decisions this week, and when I do, it will be with proper advice and a clear head.

qa.q: What had Tejas moved to a new company?
qa.a: Tejas had moved the customer list to a new company.

qa.q: Why did Vinita doubt everything after the discovery?
qa.a: Tejas was a close friend before becoming co-founder, so the betrayal made Vinita question the late nights, the first client and even the jokes.

qa.q: What steps did Vinita take instead of reacting online?
qa.a: Vinita let sadness come first, collected facts such as dates, emails and the founders' agreement, and put off big decisions until a clear head and proper advice.

qa.q: What would change if Vinita had posted online in anger?
qa.a: It could have turned a private betrayal into a public fight, harming Vinita's own work too and closing off calmer options.

grounding: A co-founder who was a close friend has betrayed Vinita; Vinita separates the sting from the value of the work, gathers facts and avoids panic decisions.

passage:
Let me tell you about the worst week of my working life. I'm Jahnavi, and three years ago Uday and I started a small organic snack company from my parents' garage. He was my college best friend. We did everything together, even fought about fonts together.

Last month I found out he had been meeting an investor alone. He'd told them he was the founder and I was "on the team". I found out from the investor's email.

My first reaction was panic. I wanted to shut down the company account, post on social media, walk away. I felt like a fool. Everything we'd built felt fake.

My mentor made me sit down. "The sting is real. The product is also real. Separate them."

So I did. I gathered every email, every invoice with my name. I asked Uday for a meeting with a lawyer present, to write down who owns what. I was sad, and I let myself be. I didn't make one big decision in panic.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi find out about Uday's investor meetings?
qa.a: She found out from the investor's email.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling when she found out?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt panic and betrayal, like a fool, as though everything they had built was fake.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi's mentor help her do?
qa.a: Separate the sting of betrayal from the real value of the work, so Jahnavi gathered facts, asked for a written agreement with a lawyer, and avoided panic decisions.

qa.q: How might Uday see his meetings with the investor?
qa.a: We can't be sure; he may have seen it as helping the company, but he chose to present himself as the only founder.

grounding: A spoken account shows someone whose co-founder and close friend broke their trust, who separates the sting from the work's value, gathers facts and documents agreements instead of panicking.

passage:
Monday. Farhan opened the company bank statement for the tea-delivery startup and saw it: three payments from the company account to Manoj's personal account, marked "consulting". No one had agreed to them. Manoj had been his friend since class eight. Farhan sat in the tiny office feeling the floor tilt. Was any of it real?

Wednesday. He almost called Manoj at midnight to shout. Instead he made a list: dates, amounts, the shareholders' agreement they had never properly finished. He spoke to their chartered accountant and asked what documents they needed.

The following Monday. Farhan met Manoj with the accountant present. "I need to understand these payments." Manoj went pale, then said he'd meant to explain. Farhan stayed calm. "Maybe. From now on, every payment needs both our signatures, and we sign the agreement this month."

That night Farhan felt sad, not panicked. The friendship was bruised. The business, and the customers who loved their tea, were still real.

qa.q: How were the payments to Manoj's personal account marked?
What was Farhan feeling when he first saw the payments?
qa.a: Farhan felt shocked and betrayed, as if the floor was tilting, doubting that any of it was real.

qa.q: What did Farhan do instead of calling Manoj at midnight?
qa.a: He gathered facts, spoke to the accountant, and later met Manoj with the accountant present to set two signatures and a written agreement.

qa.q: How did Manoj react when Farhan asked about the payments?
qa.a: Manoj went pale and said he had meant to explain, which suggests he was caught out and uneasy.

grounding: The story shows a young man whose co-founder and old friend misused company money, who separates the sting from the business's value, gathers facts and documents agreements calmly.
